video_title: What's a Revolution in Military Affairs Good For?
gist: War on the Rocks panel (Ryan Evans with Mike Horowitz, Ben Jensen and Stacie Pettyjohn) argues the 'revolution in military affairs' label is mostly unhelpful hype. They say the real shift is cheap, commercial, diffused precision ('precise/affordable mass'), which threatens exquisite US forces, rewards industrial producibility, and brings back proxy wars and punishment campaigns. They also discuss DAWG/Autonomous Warfare Command funding and AI targeting (Maven in Epic Fury).

insights.claim: The panel argues that calling something a revolution in military affairs (RMA) mostly gets in the way: the 1990s-2000s RMA debate over precision, satellites and the 'lifting of the fog of war' bent procurement rhetoric (the Marine Corps once called new boots revolutionary to get them funded), even though the capabilities themselves did come true.
insights.speaker: Mike Horowitz
insights.so_what: 'Revolutionary' rhetoric is a funding-pitch tool and a poor guide to what to buy.
insights.quote: Every time I think we talk about revolutions and like use that phrase, I think it delays the change that we want to see.

insights.claim: A panelist argues military change is slow and only looks sudden because battlefield defeat makes it look that way; real revolutions require wholesale institutional, cultural and doctrinal change, which is why Clifford Rogers' 1993 punctuated-equilibrium argument still holds.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Adoption timelines, not technology, set the pace of military advantage.
insights.quote: Military change is slow. Battlefield defeat makes it seem sudden.

insights.claim: A panelist argues current drone/AI developments are not yet a revolution because a revolution needs a large improvement in battlefield efficacy, and commercial, easily copied technology makes lasting advantage hard to achieve.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Commercial diffusion may produce a constant adaptation race rather than a decisive edge.
insights.quote: the technology is so easy to to mimic and to proliferate because it's commercial

insights.claim: Horowitz says 'drones' lumps at least four distinct categories together (collaborative combat aircraft, MALE/HALE drones like Reaper/Predator, tactical surveillance drones, and short- and long-range one-way attack munitions), so asking whether 'drones' are revolutionary is useless for procurement.
insights.speaker: Mike Horowitz
insights.so_what: Defense investors and buyers should judge drone categories separately.

insights.claim: A panelist says DIU funding something is not winning; winning is when a capability is so scaled and useful that the future force considers it old and busted.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Scaled production contracts, not prototypes, are the marker of real adoption.
insights.quote: the DIU funding something is not winning

themes.theme: Budgets, DAWG and Autonomous Warfare Command

insights.claim: Secretary Hegseth called for another $50 billion for these technologies, and the panel describes a second $50 billion for the Defense Autonomous Warfare Group (DAWG) in the FY27 budget proposal.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Large dedicated autonomy budget lines are a tailwind for drone/autonomy vendors.
insights.quote: I think this is a second 50 for the dog in the FY27 budget proposal.

insights.claim: A panelist warns that throwing money at drones without doctrine, organization and training brings sharply diminishing returns, e.g. Conex containers of drones with half-dead batteries that would have been effective two years earlier.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Short drone obsolescence cycles make bulk inventory buys risky.
insights.quote: you end up with conx containers full of drones

insights.claim: Horowitz counters that emerging capabilities like small one-way attack systems and AI have historically been underfunded, with officials in the last administration scrounging 'couch cushion money', though the services' own budgets are not following DAWG's lead, creating a bureaucratic imbalance.
insights.speaker: Mike Horowitz
insights.so_what: Service-level budget adoption is the next signal to watch beyond central initiatives.

insights.claim: A panelist reports that a 101st Airborne brigade at a JRTC rotation beat the opposing force (Geronimo) using drone-dominance initiatives and AI agents filling staff functions.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Bottom-up experimentation with drones and AI agents is showing measurable training results.

insights.claim: The panel is split on Autonomous Warfare Command (DAWG's successor): siloing drones risks weak joint integration, while leaving them to the services risks institutional resistance to uncrewed systems; success depends on money, people and a transition path to the services, and on surviving a new Congress and continuing resolutions.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Organizational durability of autonomy programs is uncertain under CR-driven funding.

insights.claim: Horowitz argues we are in an era of 'precise mass': commercial manufacturing, AI/autonomy and diffused 50-year-old precision guidance let weaker actors like the Houthis, Iran (Shaheds), Russia and Ukraine generate cheap effective strike, which flashes red for US conventional superiority.
insights.speaker: Mike Horowitz
insights.so_what: Cheap precision strike shifts the cost-exchange ratio against an exquisite US force.
insights.quote: the like lights are flashing red for like risk for American conventional military superiority

insights.claim: Horowitz says using $4 million Patriot missiles to shoot down $50,000 Shaheds is not a sustainable cost-exchange ratio.
insights.speaker: Mike Horowitz
insights.so_what: Demand should shift toward cheap counter-drone and interceptor solutions.
insights.quote: using $4 million Patriot missiles to shoot down $50,000 Shahed is not a sustainable cost exchange ratio

insights.claim: Horowitz argues that buying platforms to last 50 years (like the B-52) is a post-Cold War historical anomaly, and a return to normal means short-life systems procured, priced and produced as if kept for about 12 months.
insights.speaker: Mike Horowitz
insights.so_what: Defense procurement business models may move toward high-volume, short-cycle production.

insights.claim: A panelist argues the US industrial-base bottleneck is not technology but policy, incentives and regulation; prime-tilted market structures limit the scalable, distributed production seen in Ukraine.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Procurement reform, not new widgets, is the lever that would unlock non-prime defense production.
insights.quote: I don't think it's a technology problem. I think it's a problem of policy, incentives, regulation.

insights.claim: A panelist argues 'affordable mass' is about producibility: drones likely to be obsolete within 12 months matter less than being able to produce them in quantity quickly, on timelines current US weapons production cannot meet.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Rapid manufacturing capacity is the scarce asset in drone warfare.

insights.claim: Horowitz suggests that without 9/11, US investment would have proliferated precision battle networks and driven down costs much faster.
insights.speaker: Mike Horowitz
insights.so_what: Counter-terror spending delayed the US shift to mass-produced precision.

insights.claim: A panelist says the war in Iran, especially its early months, showed the US had not adapted institutionally to these realities fast enough.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Recent combat exposed gaps in US readiness for cheap mass threats.

themes.theme: Diffusion, proxies and the punishment era

insights.claim: A panelist frames today as the maturing of the 1990s RMA: satellite imagery, satcom and precision are now cheap, commercial and available to anyone, which is why cheap drones attacking US bases and destroying expensive aircraft looks revolutionary.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Diffusion, not new invention, is the main change in today's threat environment.

insights.claim: A panelist warns that cheap commercial weapons markets are ushering in a nasty new era of proxy warfare, citing China helping the Houthis produce cheaper ballistic missiles and North Korea sharing missiles with Russia, which strains US global commitments.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: More proxy conflict raises the costs of sustaining US global posture.

insights.claim: Research by a panelist's PhD student found drones transformed Burmese rebels' effectiveness against the military until China closed the border and cut off drone parts.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Control of commercial drone supply chains (China) is strategic leverage.

insights.claim: Analysis from the panel's firepower strike tracker finds drones are not the main problem: Shahed intercept rates, even for jet-powered variants, have not moved significantly; ballistic missiles are what get through.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Ballistic missile defense is the critical demand area, more than counter-drone.

insights.claim: A panelist expects a return to punishment campaigns against civilians and critical infrastructure, driven by cheaper ballistic missiles and rocket engines, and sketches Taiwan scenarios of graduated ballistic-missile pressure to force political concession.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Critical infrastructure and civilian targets face rising risk in future interstate wars.

insights.claim: A panelist notes India and Pakistan's recent war escalated fast and then stopped when they ran out of drones, suggesting drones can be less escalatory even while making leaders more willing to take risks.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Munition stockpile depth may cap the length of drone-centric conflicts.
insights.quote: they sort of ran out of drones and stopped

insights.claim: Horowitz says Operation Epic Fury's use of the Maven Smart System sharply increased the number of targets identified and engaged per day, and with open-source models this will spread to everyone.
insights.speaker: Mike Horowitz
insights.so_what: AI targeting is a real force multiplier, and the US lead in it will not last long.
insights.quote: it's only going to go in one direction

insights.claim: A panelist sees AI, through edge autonomy, collaborative autonomy and battle-management functions including air defense, as the most likely tipping point into a real change in warfare.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Battle-management software and autonomy are the likely high-value defense AI segments.

insights.claim: A skeptical panelist argues military AI use so far looks like 'Wile E. Coyote and Acme rockets', with more opportunity in poisoning adversary AI models and corrupting decision-making than in overcoming fog and friction.
insights.speaker: panelist
insights.so_what: Adversarial AI and model integrity may matter more than offensive AI promises.
insights.quote: it looks like wy e coyote and acme rockets
